sources.title: Ray Kroc (Q319648) -- verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-10-23): English label 'Ray Kroc', description 'American businessman', born 1902-10-05, died 1984-01-14, Korean label present, P18 'Ray Kroc 1976.jpg'. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Horatio Alger Association of Distinguished Americans, 'Ray A. Kroc' member profile (Class of 1972), read in full via fetch: founder and chairman of McDonald's Corporation; born 1902 in Oak Park, Illinois; Red Cross ambulance driver training in World War I; paper-cup salesman and piano player; national salesman for the Prince Castle Multi-Mixer; met the McDonald brothers in San Bernardino and bought the rights to franchise McDonald's nationwide; first restaurant opened 1955 in Des Plaines, Illinois; bought out the brothers in 1961 for $2.7 million; McDonald's became the world's largest fast-food chain; also owned the San Diego Padres; named among Time's 'Builders and Titans' of the 20th century. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE (an award body's short profile; it gives no year for the 1954 meeting and says nothing of standardisation or the brothers' dispute). Celebratory by design.

EBSCO Research Starters, 'Ray Kroc' (history), read in full: Kroc dropped out of high school, sold paper cups for Lily-Tulip for 17 years (rising to Midwest sales manager) and studied carry-out trends, left to sell the Multimixer in 1939, and by the early 1950s faced falling sales from imitators; he travelled to San Bernardino to see why a small drive-in bought so many Multimixers, 'Kroc did not invent fast food, nor did he found McDonald's restaurants', and chose to buy franchising rights instead of opening his own drive-in; he wrote manuals for uniform quality, incorporated at 52 and opened the Des Plaines store on 15 April 1955; early franchises failed to prosper because menus and operations differed, so he made each franchise uniform (patties ten to a pound, 1.6 ounces, 3.9 inches, a quarter ounce of onions at fifteen cents), trained owners and managers (Hamburger University, first operated in a store basement in 1961), kept franchise fees low, withdrew support from non-compliant franchisees, and let franchisees create the Big Mac, Egg McMuffin and Filet-O-Fish; the 1960s share sale made him a millionaire at 62; 'honored and vilified'; criticism of the menu and 'McDonaldization'. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE (second). Salem/EBSCO reference biography; the political-donation and philanthropy passages were not used.

Eric Pace, 'Ray A. Kroc Dies at 81; Built McDonald's Chain', The New York Times obituary, 15 January 1984, read via a reproduction on a funeral-home obituary page (the original nytimes.com page was not opened): 'a pioneer in automating and standardizing operations'; opened his first McDonald's in 1955, 7,500 outlets in the United States and 31 other countries by his death, three-quarters franchised; credited with carefully choosing franchisees skilled at personal relations, relentlessly stressing quality (banning fillers), using part-time teenage help, keeping operating costs down, and team food-preparation techniques; his eyes 'constantly checking his restaurants for cleanliness'; executives displayed his favourite dictum on persistence; notes controversies (a 1976 book alleging polygraph tests and tip appropriation, nutrition criticism) and his outspoken public rebuke of his baseball team; wrote that his huge success came late (in his 50s). Independent newspaper obituary of its time, laudatory in tone with a controversy section; its Nixon-campaign contributions and teen-wage-politics paragraphs were not used.

'Ray Kroc', Encyclopedia.com (Business Leaders, Gale/U-X-L reference biography), read in full: Kroc saw that the McDonald brothers' San Bernardino restaurant ran five Multimixers almost nonstop, quizzed diners and the brothers, proposed franchising nationwide when the brothers resisted the extra work; at 52 opened Des Plaines; kept the McDonalds' one-job-per-employee system; wanted control over franchisees but sold each only one store, did not sell supplies to them at high prices, trained them at Hamburger University; quotes Love ('the genius of Ray Kroc was that he treated franchisees as equal partners'); poured money into television advertising (Ronald McDonald from 1965); gave the brothers $2.7 million in 1961; reference-book retelling that leans on Kroc's own autobiography Grinding It Out for several episodes, so those parts are self-sourced; the passages on his health, marriages, daughter and charity were not used.

Kirkus Reviews, review of John F. Love's 'McDonald's: Behind the Arches' (1 November 1986), read in full: calls it a meticulously researched, 'definitive corporate history' that 'accentuates the positive without ignoring the implications of the rough spots'; vivid portraits of Kroc, who 'had the foresight to let franchisees and suppliers achieve wealth before him', the McDonald brothers (local pioneers of the techniques Kroc applied to mass markets) and Harry Sonneborn (credited with the real-estate base); cordial vendor relationships; more contentious franchisee relations (about 2,200 franchisees, an ombudsman appointed). Independent trade-book review of an authoritative secondary account; used because Love's book itself was not opened (lending-only); the review's characterisation is second-hand and sympathetic.

McDonald's Corporation announcement, 'Restaurant Innovator Richard McDonald Dies at 89: Pioneered McDonald's, World's Largest Restaurant System', Hotel Online Special Report, 14 July 1998, read in full: Dick and Mac McDonald opened the San Bernardino drive-in in 1940 and in 1948 rebuilt it as a limited-menu self-service restaurant (15-cent hamburgers); they franchised eight restaurants in the West before Kroc arrived; Kroc, who held the national marketing rights to the Multimixers the brothers used, was granted exclusive rights in 1955 to develop and franchise McDonald's in the United States, formed McDonald's System, Inc. in 1955 and opened the ninth McDonald's in Des Plaines in April 1955; in 1961 he bought the proprietary rights to the system, including the rest of the world; Dick McDonald was credited with the Golden Arches and 'Billions Served' signs; Fred Turner is quoted in 1987: 'Mac and Dick came up with the original design, Ray provided the foundation'. Corporate press release carried by a trade site, written by the company that Kroc built, so it is institutional and conciliatory, but it credits the brothers' prior work and corroborates the franchising chronology.

Money magazine article on the film The Founder and how the accounts of Kroc and McDonald's original founders differ (16 December 2016), read in full: recounts the 1973 TIME cover story in which Kroc says he asked for the job of franchise agent on seeing the line of customers in San Bernardino; the brothers had already franchised about six restaurants; Kroc agreed to pay them 0.5 per cent of sales and built a chain of 228 restaurants in five years; the price for the whole chain was $2.7 million with the brothers keeping their original restaurant, Kroc says it 'ended up costing me $14 million'; he told TIME 'I ran em out of business' after opening a restaurant across from the original, while Dick McDonald's letter says they renamed it themselves and that Kroc was kidding; Dick McDonald told the Wall Street Journal in 1991 that no one called Kroc the founder before the sale; the company did not honour the brothers on Founder's Day until 1991. Independent business-magazine article built on contemporaneous TIME and WSJ reporting; the contested points are presented as contested; some secondary details about dates of the autobiography are loose. CRITICAL COUNTER-VOICE on the founder claim and the buyout.

persistence.rationale: [src_kroc_ebsco, src_kroc_nyt_obit, src_kroc_encyclopedia | 1920s-1960s | reference biography + newspaper obituary] Kroc held a long sales career (17 years with Lily-Tulip, then years selling the Multimixer, with false starts in a music store and Florida real estate), launched McDonald's franchising at 52, and the early franchises failed to prosper before he standardised them; the New York Times obituary notes his success came late and that executives displayed his persistence dictum. The long stretch of work through setbacks is documented across independent summaries, but the dictum and several episodes are his own account and the tone of the sources is admiring, so the score and confidence stay moderate.

opportunity_sensing.rationale: [src_kroc_ebsco, src_kroc_encyclopedia, src_kroc_money | 1954-1955 | reference biography + business magazine] A supplier who saw an unusually large Multimixer order travelled to San Bernardino, judged that the brothers' system could be replicated, asked for the franchise-agent role and, per EBSCO, chose franchising over opening his own drive-in. The sensing of the opening is documented in two independent summaries, but the vivid details come from Kroc's own TIME and autobiography accounts, and the brothers had already franchised restaurants, so the idea of franchising was not his alone. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 74 / 0.60 because the strongest detail rests on Kroc's own telling and the brothers' earlier franchising limits his originality.

systems_abstraction.rationale: [src_kroc_ebsco, src_kroc_nyt_obit, src_kroc_hotelonline | 1955-1961 | reference biography + obituary + company release] Kroc turned the brothers' restaurant method into manuals and uniform specifications (patty weight, onions, price, potato handling), a training school and a franchise model with limited franchise sizes, and the New York Times calls him a pioneer in automating and standardising operations. The system itself originated with Dick and Mac McDonald (the company release and Kirkus credit them), so the score is for generalising and enforcing it at scale rather than inventing it; moderate confidence because the sources are summaries.

detail_orientation.rationale: [src_kroc_nyt_obit, src_kroc_ebsco | 1955-1984 | newspaper obituary + reference biography] The obituary describes his eyes 'constantly checking his restaurants for cleanliness' and his relentless insistence on quality, including banning filler ingredients, and EBSCO lists exact patty and topping specifications and withdrawal of support from franchisees who ignored the rules. The behaviour is specific, but the only direct witness description is one obituary writer's portrait of a famous man, so the confidence is moderate.

collaboration.rationale: [src_kroc_kirkus, src_kroc_encyclopedia, src_kroc_money, src_kroc_hotelonline | 1955-1991 | book review + reference biography + business magazine + company release] Love is quoted as saying Kroc treated franchisees as equal partners and Kirkus says he let franchisees and suppliers get rich before him, and the company credits him with a foundation that the brothers' design needed; against this, Dick McDonald said he was not called founder before the sale, resented the later founder claim, and Kroc's own TIME remark that he 'ran em out of business' is disputed by Dick McDonald as facetious. Partnership with franchisees is described only by admiring secondary accounts and the breakdown with the brothers is contested, so this is an inference at modest confidence and dual-edged.

portrait.source: Wikimedia Commons 'Ray Kroc und Jürgen Knauss.jpg': photograph credited to Sigfried Rödig (source: Knauss Verlag), licensed CC BY-SA 4.0 on the file page with a VRT permission ticket (2020031010005709) recorded there; used on the English and German Wikipedia pages for Ray Kroc and Jürgen Knauss. Shows Kroc (right, older man) in conversation with Jürgen Knauss (left); identity rests on the Commons/Wikipedia caption and was checked against the 1976 Padres press photo (same man). CAVEAT: the file page gives no exact photograph date (only a 2011 metadata timestamp); Knauss's German Wikipedia biography says he met Kroc in 1971 and Kroc died in 1984, so the photograph dates from roughly 1971-1984 (apparently 1970s). Cropped to the Kroc half of the 3043 x 2080 original (1300 x 1540 crop) and downscaled to 1013 x 1200; no upscaling. Derivative of a CC BY-SA 4.0 work, so the cropped file stays CC BY-SA 4.0 (ShareAlike). Supersedes the rejected eBay-sourced 'Ray Kroc 1976.jpg'.

provenance.notes: PREFLIGHT: QID VERIFIED LIVE: Wikidata wbgetentities (2026-10-23) for Q319648 returned en label 'Ray Kroc', description 'American businessman', born 1902-10-05, died 1984-01-14, P18 'Ray Kroc 1976.jpg'; the lead's hint was correct. SLUG/QID CHECK: no production or candidate file for slug ray-kroc or QID Q319648 (grep over src and data-pipeline). REGION: north_america, nationalityCodes US (born in Oak Park, Illinois, career in Chicago and San Diego). VOCABULARY: occupations entrepreneur and executive, field business, impact domains entrepreneurial and industrial, tags systematic_thinker and late_recognition and archetype entrepreneurial_builder all exist with labels; the 'founder' tag was deliberately not used because the sources agree he did not found the McDonald's restaurant concept. ZERO POLITICS: his donations to a presidential campaign and the related teen-wage controversy are unscored and excluded, as are his marriages, health, family and charity; his ownership of the San Diego Padres (a side venture) is not carded. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Horatio Alger Association profile (read) and EBSCO Research Starters 'Ray Kroc' (read in full). READ (7 cited non-Wikidata sources): Horatio Alger profile, EBSCO Research Starters, New York Times obituary 1984 (via a funeral-home reproduction), Encyclopedia.com, Kirkus review of Love's book, McDonald's release on Richard McDonald in Hotel Online, Money magazine article relaying 1973 TIME and 1991 WSJ. PERSPECTIVES: award-body and reference biography, newspaper obituary and book-review press, company release, and the McDonald brothers' account via Money (counter-voice on the founder claim and the 1961 buyout). Behavioural non-self evidence: NYT obituary, EBSCO, Kirkus. Self material: Kroc's 'Grinding It Out' and TIME interview remarks appear only secondhand and are marked as such. NOT OPENED: Love's 'McDonald's: Behind the Arches' (lending-only), 'Grinding It Out', the original NYT page (reproduction used), Tampa Bay Times 1998 obituary of Dick McDonald (paywalled; only its 1991 quotation reached me through a search summary and was not used), Time 100 essay (not found), the London Business School article (only intro retrieved), Hospitality Hall of Honor page (404), Britannica (bot block). EXCLUSIONS: Nixon contributions and teen-wage politics; allegations in the 1976 book are noted in a source but not scored. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): the three highest-risk rows reviewed were opportunity sensing (single-account detail from Kroc's own telling), persistence (partly his dictum, admiring sources) and collaboration (contested and one-sided praise); opportunity sensing was lowered from 74/0.60 to 70/0.55 because the vivid detail is Kroc's own telling and the brothers had already franchised; persistence was kept because the structural facts (17 years of sales, late start, early franchise failures) are independent; collaboration was already set at 58/0.45 as dual-edged. PORTRAIT HELD: see portrait.reason; no portrait file was downloaded or added to the repo.
